analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax credits, high-risk pools, and looser insurance rules.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act and replace it with private-insurance tax credits and high-risk pools died in committee without a cosponsor, a markup, or a vote in the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act and the health provisions of the 2010 companion law, restoring the law as it stood before 2010. In its place, it would create a refundable tax credit for low-income people to buy private insurance — but only in states that run a high-risk pool for people with pre-existing conditions — and give states $300 million a year in block grants for those pools. It would also authorize association health plans and individual membership associations that override state benefit mandates, let insurers sell coverage nationwide under the rules of one chosen state, cap malpractice damages, and pay for it partly by rescinding unspent 2009 stimulus funds.
analysis.who_benefits: Lower-income people who buy their own private insurance would get a refundable tax credit (phasing down above twice the poverty line, capped at $2,000 per adult plus $500 per dependent, with only two dependents counted). People with pre-existing conditions could access state high-risk pools backed by federal grants — but only in states that choose to run one. Small employers could claim a credit of up to $1,500 for setting up automatic enrollment, and medical students and primary care providers would get new loan support. Physicians, drug and device makers, and business associations would gain from malpractice limits, protection from comparative-effectiveness coverage decisions, and new plan-sponsoring authority.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable, advanceable tax credit for low-income individuals' private health insurance premiums, phasing down from 100% as income rises above 200% of the poverty line and capping coverage at $2,000 per adult ($4,000 joint) plus $500 per dependent, with no more than two dependents counted. [S3]
Conditions the credit on a state operating a high-risk pool, reinsurance pool, or other risk-adjustment mechanism, and provides $300 million per year in block grants to states for those pools. [S3]

Authorizes association health plans under ERISA and individual membership associations under the Public Health Service Act, both of which are exempted from certain state benefit-coverage requirements, and lets individual-market coverage follow the rules of a 'primary state' chosen by the issuer even when sold in other states. [S2]

Limits noneconomic and punitive damages in health care lawsuits, sets a statute of limitations, allows an affirmative defense for following best-practice guidelines, and gives doctors a bad-debt deduction for uncompensated care. [S2]
Prohibits the HHS Secretary from using comparative effectiveness research to deny coverage of any item or service under a federal health care program. [S2]

Gives small employers a credit of up to $1,500 for establishing automatic enrollment and a defined-contribution health option, and funds student loan and repayment programs for medical professionals. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions would depend on high-risk pools with $300 million in total annual federal funding — historically a thin substitute for guaranteed coverage — and those in states without a pool would get no credit at all. Patients injured by malpractice would face caps on non-economic and punitive damages and a shorter window to sue. Consumers would lose state benefit mandates wherever coverage is sold through associations or across state lines under another state's rules. Children in families above 300% of the poverty line would be barred from CHIP payments, and the offsets come from rescinding unspent stimulus funds and imposing new discretionary spending limits.

drawbacks.text: Repeal restores the pre-2010 legal landscape, in which insurers could deny coverage or charge unaffordable rates for pre-existing conditions; the bill's answer is a high-risk-pool system that states must opt into, funded at $300 million per year nationwide, and people in non-participating states lose even the tax credit. [S2] [S3]

The malpractice title caps non-economic and punitive damages and shortens the limitations period, which reduces compensation for patients with serious injuries; the bill offers no federal floor of coverage protections to offset the interstate-sale and association-plan preemptions of state benefit laws. [S2]

CHIP payments would be prohibited for children in families above 300% of the poverty line, and states would have to show how they will reach only 90% of targeted low-income children — a narrowing of the existing program. [S2]

An honest supporter would also acknowledge that the credit is modest — it covers only two dependents and phases out steeply above 200% of poverty, so the replacement likely covers fewer people at greater out-of-pocket cost than the law it repeals. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the Affordable Care Act's coverage expansions and consumer protections for a narrower credit-plus-high-risk-pool design whose funding and eligibility limits are far below what the ACA provided. Some pieces — the refundable credit, small-employer credit, and loan support for medical professionals — would help real people. But the cost falls on the people least able to bear it: those with pre-existing conditions in states that skip the pools, children above 300% of poverty in CHIP, and malpractice victims facing damage caps. As drafted, the costs outweigh the benefits for the households that the ACA most directly helped.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to ten House committees and then six subcommittees in early 2011, and it never received a markup, a hearing-based vote, or floor action before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Burton introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress. [S1] [S5]

It was referred to ten House committees — Energy and Commerce, Budget, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, House Administration, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Rules, Appropriations, and Oversight and Government Reform. [S5]

Between January 24 and February 25, 2011, it was referred to six subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions. [S5]
The bill had no cosponsors at any point. [S4]
No further action of any kind appears in the record through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2013 — no committee vote, no House vote, no Senate action. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People covered by the Affordable Care Act's provisions — including its pre-existing-condition protections and coverage expansions — kept them for the rest of the 112th Congress, because this repeal-and-replace bill never advanced. No interest group's alternative became law either; the ACA simply remained in force while repeal attempts failed to attract enough support, even in a chamber with a Republican majority. The lack of a single cosponsor signaled that no member of either party wanted to attach their name to this specific version.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on the ACA's protections

against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond subcommittee referrals — no markup, no committee vote, no report — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor in two years, despite the chamber's Republican majority.

sides.party_line_note: The only sponsor was a Republican and no member of either party cosponsored, but the record contains no votes, so the partisan split on this specific bill cannot be measured.

industries.note: Repealing the ACA strips away its coverage rules and subsidized customer base, but the replacement again routes public subsidies through private insurers — advance tax-credit payments go directly to insurers — and hands them new sales channels through association plans, IMAs, and nationwide sale under one state's rules. Insurers gain freedom from regulation while keeping their role as the channel for publicly supported coverage, and consumers bear the weakened protections.

The HEALTH Act title caps noneconomic and punitive damages, shortens the limitations period, and lets compliance with best-practice guidelines serve as a defense, reducing malpractice exposure; the direct cost of those caps falls on injured patients. A bad-debt deduction partially offsets doctors' uncompensated-care costs.

The bill bars HHS from using comparative effectiveness research to deny coverage of any item or service under federal health programs, shielding products from cost-based coverage limits. The added cost lands on federal health spending and the taxpayers who fund it.

industries.industry: Trade associations and chambers of commerce
industries.note: Both titles creating association health plans and individual membership associations hand established business associations new authority to sponsor health coverage exempted from some state benefit mandates. Members could get cheaper options, but the preemptions also strip state-mandated benefits.
